title: DECODING MODERN ARCHITECTURE A Lens Model Approach for Understanding the Aesthetic Differences of Architects and Laypersons
central_proposition: The modified lens model provides a useful framework for understanding how architects and laypersons formulate aesthetic appraisals of buildings, specifically by identifying the distinct physical features and emotional responses that underlie their differing global evaluations.

concept_definitions.name: Lens Model
concept_definitions.definition: A useful and unified framework for displaying the ways in which different groups respond to particular objective features of the physical environment, integrate these reactions into emotional impressions, and translate the emotional impressions into an overall aesthetic evaluation of a building.

concept_definitions.name: Physical Cues (Distal Cues)
concept_definitions.definition: Objective, observable elements of building exteriors (e.g., number of stories, percentage of glass, metal cladding) that observers use to form judgments.

concept_definitions.name: Emotional Responses
concept_definitions.definition: Affective reactions to buildings, specifically measured along the orthogonal dimensions of pleasure (ranging from ugly to beautiful) and arousal (ranging from unarousing to intense).

concept_definitions.name: Global Aesthetic Appraisal
concept_definitions.definition: An observer's overall subjective evaluation of a building's aesthetic quality, ranging from 'terrible architecture' to 'excellent architecture'.

concept_definitions.name: Formal Aesthetics
concept_definitions.definition: Cognitive concepts related to goodness of fit or prototypicality in architectural appraisal.

argument_structure: The paper introduces the long-standing problem of architect-layperson disagreement in architectural aesthetics, reviews existing research approaches, and proposes the modified lens model as a comprehensive framework to investigate the physical and emotional bases of these differences. It then describes an empirical study applying this model to modern office buildings, presents the results showing distinct cue utilization and emotional pathways for each group, and discusses how these findings clarify the observed divergence in aesthetic appraisals.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The lens model posits a causal chain where objective physical features (distal cues) of a building are perceived by observers, leading to specific emotional responses (pleasure and arousal). These emotional responses, in turn, mediate the observer's global aesthetic appraisal of the building. Differences in aesthetic appraisals between groups (e.g., architects and laypersons) arise from differences in which physical cues they attend to, how they integrate these cues into emotional impressions, or how they translate emotional impressions into global appraisals.

findings.consequent: Predictable affective responses (pleasure, arousal) in observers
findings.mechanism: Observers process objective building characteristics, which directly evoke specific emotional states.
findings.quote: First, it aims to demonstrate that particular physical features of buildings produce predictable affective responses in observers.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This study found that for architects, pleasure was significantly related to more metal cladding (r=.57), fewer arches (r=-.31), and more railings (r=.33). Architects' arousal was related to fancy (r=.54), metal cladding (r=.41), rounded corners (r=.30), and triangular elements (r=.34). For laypersons, arousal was related to more glass (r=.50), greater reflectivity (r=.48), more fenestration (r=.46), more stories (r=.42), less color uniformity (r=-.35), and fancy (r=.35). No physical cues were significantly related to laypersons' pleasure.

findings.mechanism: Emotional states elicited by the environment directly inform and influence overall aesthetic judgments.
findings.quote: Second, it seeks to show that these affective responses are in turn reliably associated with observers' global evaluations of buildings.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This study found that for both architects and laypersons, global assessments were very strongly and positively related to building-elicited pleasure (r=.51 and r=.86, respectively). Arousal was not significantly correlated with global impression for either group.

findings.antecedent: Different sets of objective building features used by different observer groups (architects vs. laypersons)
findings.consequent: Divergence in aesthetic evaluations (emotional assessments and global appraisals)
findings.mechanism: Distinct processing of environmental cues by different observer groups leads to varied emotional and aesthetic outcomes, resulting in low agreement on global appraisals.
findings.quote: the two groups based their emotional assessments on almost entirely different sets of objective building features, which may help to explain why the aesthetic evaluations of architects and laypersons are virtually unrelated.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This study found that architects and laypersons based their emotional assessments on almost entirely different sets of objective building features. Consequently, their global assessments (r=.14) and rated pleasure (r=-.08) were virtually unrelated.

findings.antecedent: Shared utilization of physical cues by different observer groups
findings.consequent: Higher agreement in global aesthetic appraisals
findings.mechanism: Common processing pathways for environmental information lead to convergent aesthetic judgments.
findings.quote: In general, the lens model predicts that more agreement between groups will be observed when both groups use the same physical cues in the same way to reach their conclusions.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This study found that architects and laypersons did significantly agree about the arousal-eliciting qualities of the 42 buildings (r=.54), and shared only one physical cue (fanciness) as a basis for their arousal appraisals. This partial overlap in cue utilization for arousal contrasts with the almost entirely different cues used for pleasure, which resulted in low agreement on pleasure and global ratings.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The lens framework can explain how the appraisals of architects and laypersons diverge by identifying the specific physical cues and emotional responses relied upon by each group.

Analyses using the lens model can reveal whether the emotional impact of buildings on architects derives from different building features than on nonarchitects, or if both groups derive their overall aesthetic appraisals from the same (or different) emotional responses.
Information derived from the lens model about the bases of lay preferences can be used by architects to predict lay responses to their work, potentially increasing lay satisfaction.
The lens model can be used to educate laypersons about the reasons architects prefer certain buildings that laypersons might find unattractive.
bridge_warrants: The lens model framework integrates with Mehrabian and Russell's (1974) pleasure-arousal model of affect, using these dimensions to characterize emotional responses to buildings.

The lens model approach can be connected to hypotheses that layperson-architect differences are related to their different conceptualizations of buildings at a more abstract level, such as prototypicality of style or richness of materials.
methodological_critiques: Previous research on architect-layperson differences often showed that groups differ in their assessments or conceptualizations of buildings, but did not fully investigate the specific physical and emotional bases for these disagreements.

A main criticism of research in environmental psychology has been the lack of attention to specific physical attributes of settings, which the lens model addresses by grounding research in objective building features.
model_structure: The lens model (Figure 1) illustrates hypothetical links between physical (distal) cues, emotional responses (pleasure and arousal), and global impressions of buildings. It depicts separate, mirror-image pathways for architects and laypersons, allowing for group-specific relationships between cues, emotions, and global appraisals. An agreement index quantifies the similarity of judgments between groups.
limitations: Not all 59 initially identified TACS cues could be reliably rated, with only 25 meeting the minimum interrater agreement criterion of .70, potentially limiting the scope of physical features investigated.

The study found that laypersons' pleasure ratings were not significantly related to any of the 25 examined building cues, suggesting that other unmeasured cues might be important for layperson pleasure.
While architects and laypersons shared 'fanciness' as a cue for arousal, other cues contributing to their arousal appraisals might not have been among the 25 investigated in this study.
Complete uniformity in photographic angle and style for the building slides could not be attained, which might introduce minor variability.

Nonbuilding context variables (landscaping, roads, human presence) were found to have little impact on assessments in this study, suggesting the model's focus on facades might miss broader contextual influences.

The study acknowledges that observers likely create categories and prototypes from physical attributes, suggesting a need for future research to link the current approach with more abstract conceptualizations of building meaning (e.g., styles, schemas).

The study design aimed for sufficient inter-observer agreement, implying that the number of observers was chosen to stabilize group-level ratings, but individual differences within groups (especially laypersons) are noted as a factor.

The linear model of arousal's relationship to global assessment was not significant for either group, though a second-order (quadratic) relationship for arousal was mildly related to global assessment among laypersons, suggesting a more complex dose-response for arousal than initially modeled.

paper_metadata.title: Decoding Modern Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The physical and affective bases of the differences between architects’ and laypersons’ aesthetic evaluations of building facades were examined. Fifty-nine objective features of 42 large modern office buildings were related to ratings of the buildings’ emotional impact and global aesthetic quality made by architects and laypersons. Both groups strongly based their global assessments on elicited pleasure (and not on elicited arousal), but the two groups based their emotional assessments on almost entirely different sets of objective building features, which may help to explain why the aesthetic evaluations of architects and lay persons are virtually unrelated.

crossref_abstract: The physical and affective bases of the differences between architects’ and laypersons’ aesthetic evaluations of building facades were examined. Fifty-nine objective features of 42 large modern office buildings were related to ratings of the buildings’ emotional impact and global aesthetic quality made by architects and laypersons. Both groups strongly based their global assessments on elicited pleasure (and not on elicited arousal), but the two groups based their emotional assessments on almost entirely different sets of objective building features, which may help to explain why the aesthetic evaluations of architects and lay persons are virtually unrelated.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The Lens Model can be applied to understand how architects and laypersons make aesthetic judgments of modern architecture by analyzing their differential utilization and weighting of probabilistic physical features (cues) of buildings.
